text: Best Buy Co., Inc. was incorporated in Minnesota in 1966 and operates in the United States and Canada, driven by its purpose to enrich lives through technology and its vision to personalize and humanize technology solutions for every stage of life. The company operates through two reportable segments: Domestic and International. The Domestic segment includes all U.S. states, districts, and territories, as well as Best Buy Health, and encompasses brand names such as Best Buy, Best Buy Ads, Best Buy Business, Best Buy Health, CST, Current Health, Geek Squad, Lively, Magnolia, Pacific Kitchen and Home, TechLiquidators, and Yardbird, along with domain names bestbuy.com, currenthealth.com, lively.com, techliquidators.com, and yardbird.com. All of Best Buy’s former stores in Mexico were closed by the end of the first quarter of fiscal 2022, and the International segment consists of all operations in Canada under the brands Best Buy, Best Buy Mobile, and Geek Squad, and the domain bestbuy.ca. In fiscal 2022, the company acquired all outstanding shares of Current Health Ltd. and Two Peaks, LLC d/b/a Yardbird Furniture. Both segments operate an omnichannel platform enabling customers to shop online, visit stores, or have services delivered to their homes. Key business functions such as merchandise development, pricing, procurement, supply chain, marketing, and labor deployment are centrally managed, while support functions like human resources, finance, IT, and real estate are based at corporate headquarters. Field operations support retail, services, and in-home teams from corporate and regional locations. Store operations follow standardized procedures with flexibility for local market adjustments. The Best Buy Health business has a dedicated leadership and operations team that manages daily operations with support from enterprise capabilities. Revenue is generated through six categories: Computing and Mobile Phones, Consumer Electronics, Appliances, Entertainment, Services, and Other. Online customers can choose to pick up products at a Best Buy store, at an alternative location, or have them delivered directly to their homes, with a ship-from-store capability improving availability and delivery times. Most merchandise is shipped directly from manufacturers to distribution centers. In fiscal 2023, the company’s 20 largest suppliers accounted for approximately 79% of merchandise purchased, with Apple, Samsung, HP, LG, and Sony representing about 57% of total purchases. The company does not have long-term written contracts with vendors and manages inventory through continuous monitoring of demand, adjusting receipt levels and pricing, and agreements on markdown reimbursements and return privileges. A global sourcing operation designs, develops, tests, and contracts the manufacture of exclusive brand products. As of the end of fiscal 2023, Best Buy operated 1,138 stores across its Domestic and International segments, which are central to its omnichannel strategy and competitive advantage. The company also offers vendor store-within-a-store concepts to strengthen vendor partnerships and enhance the customer experience, and continuously evaluates store space, leases, and locations. Best Buy owns or has rights to use valuable intellectual property, including trademarks and service marks such as Best Buy, Geek Squad, Lively, Magnolia, Pacific Kitchen and Home, and others, and holds patents for many of its inventions. The company is committed to environmental sustainability, aiming to advance the circular economy, reduce waste, promote sustainable products, and transition to renewable energy, having invested in five solar fields by the end of fiscal 2023 to support its carbon reduction goals. The business is seasonal, with a significant portion of revenue and earnings generated in the fiscal fourth quarter, which includes the holiday shopping season. Operations are funded through available cash, cash equivalents, operating cash flows, and revolving credit facilities used for working capital, general corporate purposes, investments, and growth. Working capital needs increase before the holiday season due to inventory purchases. Competitors include multi-channel retailers, e-commerce businesses, technology service providers, traditional retailers, vendors, and mobile network carriers. Best Buy’s competitive advantages include its ability to serve customers online, in stores, and at home, integrated technology solutions, broad product assortment, strong vendor partnerships, service offerings tailored to customer needs, unique store formats, and efficient supply chain operations. The company monitors competitor pricing and offers price-matching policies to maintain competitiveness. The Nominating, Corporate Governance and Public Policy Committee of the Board of Directors oversees the effectiveness and risks of the company’s environmental, social, and governance strategy, including environmental goals, social responsibility programs, and public policy initiatives. As of March 15, 2023, the company had 218,045,737 shares of common stock, $0.10 par value per share, issued and outstanding. The aggregate market value of the voting and non-voting common equity held by non-affiliates as of July 29, 2022, was approximately $13.4 billion, based on a share price of $76.99, as reported on the New York Stock Exchange-Composite Index. All of the company’s directors and executive officers are considered affiliates for this calculation. The report is filed pursuant to Section 13 or 15(d) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 for the fiscal year ended January 28, 2023, and includes portions of the Definitive Proxy Statement for the 2023 Regular Meeting of Shareholders, which will be filed with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission within 120 days after the fiscal year-end. The document includes forward-looking statements that are subject to risks and uncertainties, with a description of key factors outlined in Item 1A, Risk Factors.

Our competitive advantage is built on a broad and curated product assortment, strong vendor partnerships, service and support offerings that address real customer needs, our unique ability to showcase technology in distinct store formats, and a robust supply chain. We are committed to enriching lives through technology while positively impacting the environment, communities, and stakeholders, including customers, employees, vendors, and shareholders. The Nominating, Corporate Governance and Public Policy Committee of the Board oversees our environmental, social, and governance strategy, including environmental goals, social responsibility programs, and public policy initiatives. We aim to advance the circular economy by conserving natural resources, reducing waste, offering sustainable products, and transitioning to renewable energy. As of the end of fiscal 2023, we have invested in five solar fields to support our carbon reduction goals. We target a 75% reduction in carbon emissions by 2030 (over a 2009 baseline) and carbon neutrality by 2040, achieved through energy efficiency, renewable energy deployment, fleet electrification, and emission neutralization. We also aim to reduce water consumption by 15% by 2025 (over a 2019 baseline) and achieve zero-waste certification at additional distribution centers. We expect our ENERGY STAR® products to help customers reduce carbon emissions by 20% by 2030 (over a 2017 baseline), saving them at least $5 billion in utility costs. We support the circular economy through repair and trade-in services and an electronics and appliance recycling program, having collected more than 2.7 billion pounds of such materials since 2009, including over 183 million pounds in fiscal 2023. In social matters, we uphold human rights and responsible sourcing through alignment with the United Nations Guiding Principles and our Responsible Sourcing Program, participating in the Responsible Business Alliance with brands like Apple, Intel, Microsoft, and Samsung, and adhering to a shared Supplier Code of Conduct and audit methodology. The Best Buy Foundation supports 52 Best Buy Teen Tech Center® locations and aims to reach 100 by 2025, offering teens access to cutting-edge technology, post-secondary guidance, mentors, social and emotional support, and paid internships. At the end of fiscal 2023, we employed more than 90,000 employees in the U.S. and Canada, with approximately 58% full-time, 32% part-time, and 10% seasonal/occasional. We set diversity goals for fiscal 2025 and achieved 37% of new salaried corporate positions and 25% of new salaried field positions with Black, Indigenous and People of Color (BIPOC) employees, meeting our one-in-three target. We are committed to spending at least $1.2 billion with BIPOC and diverse businesses by 2025 and investing up to $10 million with Brown Venture Group, a firm focused on Black, Latino, and Indigenous technology startups. We also plan to spend $44 million by 2025 to expand college preparation and career opportunities for BIPOC students, including scholarships for Historically Black Colleges and Universities and increased funding for Best Buy Teen Tech Center youth. The Compensation and Human Resources Committee oversees human capital policies, while the Nominating, Corporate Governance and Public Policy Committee includes diversity considerations in Board candidate selection. In fiscal 2023, each U.S. employee spent an average of at least 44 hours on training and development, with enhancements including expanded leadership development, an AI-driven workforce planning program, LinkedIn Learning for full-time employees, and a new onboarding training program. Employee benefits include caregiver support for disabilities and neurodivergence via Joshin, caregiver support through Wellthy for emergency housing, healthcare, substance abuse, and eldercare, pay continuation and caregiver pay, 10 weeks of maternity leave at 100% pay, Included Health for LGBTQ+ needs, access to virtual physical and mental health visits, emergency assistance through the HOPE Fund (up to $2,500), mental health awareness and training, and tuition assistance with expanded partnerships for degree attainment at no out-of-pocket cost. The Compensation and Human Resources Committee reviews employee wellness, engagement, benefit compliance, leadership succession, wage, retention, and hiring programs. For more information on environmental, social, and governance matters, see Best Buy’s Fiscal 2023 Environmental, Social and Governance Report, including a Task Force for Climate Related Financial Disclosures index expected in June 2023, available at https://corporate.bestbuy.com/sustainability. We are subject to Exchange Act reporting requirements and file annual, quarterly, and current reports with the SEC, which are available free of charge on our investor website at https://investors.bestbuy.com. We also post our Articles of Incorporation, By-laws, Corporate Governance Principles, Code of Business Ethics, and committee charters on the same site. Copies of these documents can be requested free of charge to Best Buy Co., Inc. Investor Relations Department at 7601 Penn Avenue South, Richfield, MN 55423-3645. We disclose information through our websites, including https://bestbuy.com for products and services, https://investors.bestbuy.com for investment-related content, and https://corporate.bestbuy.com/archive/ for press releases. These websites are not incorporated by reference into this report. Item 1A outlines risk factors categorized as external, strategic, operational, regulatory and legal, and financial and market. Key external risks include macroeconomic pressures such as geopolitical climate, inflation, consumer confidence, and oil prices, which can affect consumer spending, brand choices, device upgrades, and service demand. Geopolitical issues, such as the conflict in Ukraine, may impact fuel prices, inflation, global supply chains, and raw material costs, particularly for nickel, aluminum, and copper, due to Russia’s role as a major producer. Disruptions in supply chains or manufacturing in regions like Taiwan or China, due to tensions between Taiwan and China or other trade or political factors, could affect semiconductor and television panel production. Catastrophic events, including pandemics like COVID-19, natural disasters, extreme weather, or terrorism, can disrupt operations, supply chains, distribution networks, and IT systems, with effects amplified when occurring simultaneously. The COVID-19 pandemic has specifically impacted customer store visits, supply chain disruptions, fluctuating consumer spending, operational changes like contactless pick-up, safety standards, channel shifts to online shopping, and our ability to finance operations. The emergence of new, more transmissible SARS-COV-2 variants could worsen these risks. Three of our largest sales states—California, Texas, and Florida—are prone to natural disasters and extreme weather conditions.

The COVID-19 pandemic has introduced and may continue to introduce significant risks to the business, operations, and financial condition, including (i) reduced customer visits and spending at stores, (ii) supply chain disruptions, (iii) fluctuating consumer spending influenced by government stimulus, (iv) operational changes such as the rollout of contactless and curbside pick-up, (v) safety standards imposed by state and federal agencies, (vi) shifts in customer channels—such as increased online shopping—potentially affecting profitability, and (vii) challenges in financing operations. The emergence of new, more transmissible, virulent, or immune-evading SARS-COV-2 variants could worsen these risks. Three of the largest states by total sales—California, Texas, and Florida—have experienced and may continue to experience natural disasters and extreme weather, which could cause physical damage or closures of stores, distribution centers, or other facilities. External social activism, tension, and violence related to social justice and inequality, and the company’s response to such events, may negatively affect employees, customers, properties, and communities, potentially damaging the brand and reputation if the response is perceived as inappropriate or inadequate. Such events could lead to operational interruptions, property or inventory losses, and adverse effects on revenue and profitability. Many products sold are vulnerable to technological advancements, product life cycle changes, and shifting consumer preferences. The industry is highly dynamic, driven by rapid innovation, including new product categories, rapid category maturation, cannibalization, changing price points, and frequent product replacement or upgrades. This pace of change is difficult to predict and manage; failure to respond effectively could result in offering unwanted products, excess inventory requiring discounting, inability to secure products due to high demand, delays in adapting merchandising, marketing, or supply chain capabilities, and brand damage. The company faces strong competition from multi-channel retailers, e-commerce businesses, technology service providers, traditional retailers, vendors, and mobile network carriers, with price transparency and real-time price comparison increasing competitive pressure. Online and mobile-driven sales, including in-store or curbside pickup, are growing, and customers increasingly demand faster, guaranteed delivery and low or free shipping. The company’s higher cost structure due to its focus on superior customer service and a full range of services may pressure margins, especially as delivery costs and times become more competitive. Failure to attract, retain, and engage qualified employees—particularly in key roles—could harm operations and profitability. High turnover in the retail sector, especially during the pandemic, and market pressures to increase wages and benefits could negatively impact profitability. The company’s strategy to expand into health, new products, services, and technologies introduces business, financial, and regulatory risks, including limited experience in new markets, regulatory challenges, and potential claims from service disruptions or failures. These initiatives increase complexity in management, operations, systems, and financial controls, and pilot programs may not scale as expected, limiting growth. Healthcare-related products and services require regulatory approvals, with the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (“FDA”) regulating product safety, quality, and supplier materials; non-compliance could lead to recalls, production stoppages, fines, or legal claims. The digitalization of Best Buy Health, including handling personal and medical data, increases compliance risks under laws such as the Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act (HIPAA) and the UK’s General Data Protection Regulation (“GDPR”), exposing the company to data privacy, security, and business interruption risks. Offering a full range of services—such as consultation, delivery, installation, memberships, repair, technical support, and caregiving—introduces risks including declining service attachment due to online purchasing trends, rising labor costs, margin pressure from the Best Buy Totaltech membership (which includes incremental benefits and costs), pressure on traditional labor models, use of third parties that fail to meet labor or independent contractor standards, errors in service fulfillment, unpredictable warranty failures, increased liability from employees using company vehicles or being present in customer homes, expanded liability in managed services, access to customer devices and data, third-party involvement in construction, weather and safety-related disruptions, and non-compliance with new laws. The company relies on a wide range of domestic and international vendors, with the 20 largest suppliers accounting for approximately 79% of merchandise purchased in fiscal 2023, and five suppliers—Apple, Samsung, HP, LG, and Sony—accounting for about 57% of total purchases. Most vendor relationships lack long-term contracts, and the company depends on favorable terms for pricing, promotional funding, payment terms, product allocations, store experiences, and returns. Vendors may leverage their financial strength, brand power, or retail presence to our disadvantage, especially when purchases represent a small portion of their revenue or when competition is low. Mobile carriers, which are limited in number, also impact the business; changes in their contract structures, fee plans, or service levels could reduce new device sales and harm revenue. Declines in demand could occur if brand perception or recognition is damaged through poor service, uncompetitive pricing, missed delivery promises, or negative public remarks, with social media amplifying customer feedback and reputational harm. Third-party fraud using the brand could also harm perception. Strategic ventures, alliances, or acquisitions carry risks such as unanticipated business risks, failure to retain key employees, financial forecasting uncertainty, integration challenges, control deficiencies, failure to achieve cost synergies, environmental changes, disputes with partners, and adverse impacts on vendor or partner relationships; failure could impair liquidity, profitability, and require goodwill or asset impairments, while diverting resources and management focus. Poor management of the real estate portfolio—such as failing to secure suitable store locations or adjusting to changing consumer behavior—could impair competitiveness and profitability. Most properties are under multi-year leases, and key evaluation factors include customer behavior, store format, product mix, local competition, demographics, lease terms, and occupancy costs. Failure to properly assess these factors or negotiate terms could result in store closures with ongoing lease obligations, significant remodeling costs, operating locations that no longer meet business needs, or excessive lease expenses. Exiting leased locations involves variable financial impacts based on lease terms, market conditions, property demand, landlord relationships, and sub-lease availability, with ongoing responsibilities for taxes, insurance, and common area maintenance on vacant properties. When sub-leasing, the company remains liable as the master lessee in case of sub-tenant default. Operational risks include interruptions to store and supply chain operations, such as delivery failures, third-party underperformance, system disruptions, capacity limits, global supply chain issues, inventory loss from theft or damage, employee or customer safety risks from burglary or robbery, transportation or distribution sector consolidation or failures, labor strikes or shortages, pandemics (including COVID-19), and rising transportation costs.

We rely on third-party vendors and partners to support critical aspects of our operations, including delivery and installation, customer warranty, information technology, web hosting, cloud services, customer loyalty programs, promotional financing, gift cards, technical support, transportation, insurance, and human resources. Any material disruption in these relationships or in the services provided by third parties could negatively affect our revenues, cost structure, and operations, especially during peak periods. Our exclusive brands products—such as Best Buy Essentials, Dynex, Insignia, Modal, Platinum, Rocketfish, Jitterbug, and Lively—are a significant part of our revenue and profitability, but most are manufactured by contract manufacturers in China and Southeast Asia, exposing us to additional risks. These include greater responsibility for warranty claims, limited recourse in foreign jurisdictions, potential regulatory or product liability claims, product recalls, manufacturing or logistics disruptions due to the COVID-19 pandemic, inconsistent order patterns, inability to form long-term manufacturer relationships, geopolitical crises like the conflict in Ukraine, inventory obsolescence without return-to-vendor rights, evolving labor and environmental laws, intellectual property infringement or royalty failures, trade disputes or tariffs, and difficulties in securing or protecting patents. We also face risks related to vendors sourcing products outside the U.S., such as political instability, trade restrictions, tariffs, quality issues, port delays, currency fluctuations, transportation costs, inflation, natural disasters, pandemics, and vendor underinvestment in facilities or pricing changes. Our business is heavily dependent on information technology systems for demand forecasting, purchasing, supply chain management, point-of-sale processing, services fulfillment, staff planning, financial management, reporting, and data security. Failures or interruptions due to power outages, cyberattacks, viruses, denial-of-service attacks, security breaches, natural disasters, or employee errors could severely disrupt operations, increase costs, and lead to lost revenue. As we migrate more systems to the cloud, we face new risks related to security, system configuration, and service reliability. We are particularly vulnerable to cybersecurity threats, data breaches, and unauthorized access to customer, employee, and vendor data, especially as online sales and remote work grow. These risks are heightened by the collection and storage of sensitive information, including payment card and health data, and by the potential for vulnerabilities in products sold or serviced. Increased costs for cybersecurity, compliance, fraud, and insurance, along with evolving state, federal, and international laws on data privacy and security, add financial and operational burdens. Product safety and quality failures could lead to legal risks, recalls, reputational damage, and reduced profitability. Changes in labor laws—such as unionization, employee classification, minimum wage, paid leave, and scheduling—could increase payroll costs and affect service delivery. We are also exposed to regulatory and legal risks, including compliance with conflicting laws, environmental regulations, product safety standards, data privacy rules, and evolving legislation in areas like finance, labor, healthcare, and corporate governance. Geopolitical tensions, especially trade disputes or tariff increases with China, could disrupt supply chains and operations. Changes in U.S. or international tax laws could negatively impact our financial condition. Regulatory activity in the retail sector increases compliance costs and risks of fines. Legal proceedings, including class-action lawsuits and labor disputes, require significant expense and management attention. Climate change concerns may lead to new regulations, higher compliance and operational costs, and shifts in consumer behavior. Additionally, evolving corporate governance and ESG regulations—such as those from the SEC, NYSE, and FASB—require increased spending and management time, and our ESG initiatives may face criticism for inaccuracy, incompleteness, or failure to meet goals. Our international operations face the same risks as domestic operations, plus country-specific legislative, judicial, regulatory, political, economic, and cultural factors. We operate retail locations in Canada.

ESG-related initiatives and goals may be difficult and expensive to implement, and the technologies required might not be cost-effective or advance at a sufficient pace. The accuracy, adequacy, or completeness of ESG disclosures could be subject to criticism, and progress toward these goals may rely on evolving standards, internal controls, and assumptions that could change. Criticism could also arise regarding the scope, nature, or revisions to these goals. If ESG data, processes, or reporting are incomplete or inaccurate, or if progress toward ESG goals is not achieved on time or at all, the company’s reputation, business, financial performance, and growth could be negatively impacted. International operations face similar risks, plus additional risks tied to local legislative, judicial, regulatory, political, economic, and cultural factors. The company operates retail locations in Canada, Current Health in the UK, and most of its exclusive brand products are manufactured by contract manufacturers in southeast Asia. It also has wholly-owned legal entities in Bermuda, China, Hong Kong, Luxembourg, the Republic of Mauritius, and the UK. During fiscal 2023, the International segment generated approximately 8% of total revenue. General risks also apply to international operations, including political instability, economic conditions such as monetary and fiscal policies, tax rules, and foreign exchange rate risk, changes in international trade rules or ownership of foreign entities, government travel restrictions (including those from the COVID-19 pandemic), cultural differences, employee relations practices (such as works councils or unions), difficulties enforcing intellectual property rights, and challenges in managing remote operations. These factors could significantly disrupt international operations and materially harm revenue, profitability, and lead to material impairments or exit costs. The company is highly dependent on cash flows and net earnings from its fiscal fourth quarter, which includes the majority of the holiday shopping season. A large portion of revenue and earnings comes from this period, which is also affected by unpredictable factors like competitive promotions, new product launches, and customer buying patterns. Unexpected events—such as pandemics, natural or man-made disasters, shifts in consumer demand, economic changes, product sourcing issues, cyber-attacks, system failures, or third-party vendor disruptions—could severely disrupt operations and negatively affect fourth-quarter and annual results. The company offers promotional financing and credit cards managed by third-party banks, which generate incremental revenue and profit-sharing income. Approximately 25% of fiscal 2023 revenue was transacted via branded cards, and the company earns income or shares losses based on program performance, influenced by transaction volume, financing terms, bad debt rates, interest rates, regulatory and competitive environments, and operating expenses. Adverse changes in these factors could reduce the availability of financing programs and lower revenue. Constraints in capital markets or tighter vendor credit terms could materially harm liquidity. The company relies on operating cash flows, available cash, liquid investments, credit facilities, debt arrangements, and trade payables to fund working capital, debt service, and business opportunities. A reduction in vendor payment terms or credit limits could threaten liquidity, and if needed, the company may seek additional financing. Liquidity depends on economic conditions, financial stability of banks, credit availability, credit ratings, and the company’s reputation with lenders—factors that could increase borrowing costs or limit access to capital. Downgrades in credit ratings could reduce market perception of credit risk, limit access to capital, and increase borrowing and lease costs. Ratings are based on company-provided information and may be revised, suspended, or withdrawn due to developments beyond the company’s control, such as changes in rating methodologies. Failure to meet public financial guidance or forward-looking statements could lead to a decline in the stock price. The company provides financial guidance to investors and analysts, which is forward-looking and subject to risks and uncertainties. Actual results may differ from guidance due to inaccurate sales forecasts, fixed expenses, and slow spending adjustments. Revenue and operating profit growth depend on demand for products and services and are affected by global economic and business conditions. If results fail to meet guidance or market expectations, or if guidance is reduced, the market price of the company’s common stock may decline. At the end of fiscal 2023, the Domestic segment had 978 stores, with a total square footage of 37,388 thousand square feet, including 20 Pacific Sales stores, 19 Best Buy Outlet Centers, and 14 Yardbird stand-alone stores. The International segment had 160 stores, with a total square footage of 3,621 thousand square feet, including 33 Best Buy Mobile stores. Ownership status showed 922 leased and 24 owned domestic locations, 32 owned buildings and 153 leased international locations with 3 owned. Distribution space totaled 14,393 thousand square feet leased and 3,168 thousand square feet owned domestically, and 1,496 thousand square feet leased internationally with no owned space. The company owns its corporate headquarters in Richfield, Minnesota, and leases additional domestic and international office space to support operations. The company’s common stock is traded on the New York Stock Exchange under the ticker symbol BBY. The Board initiated a regular quarterly cash dividend in fiscal 2004, and a quarterly dividend has been paid each subsequent quarter. On March 2, 2023, the company announced an increase in its regular quarterly dividend from $0.88 to $0.92 per share. Future dividend payments will depend on earnings, capital requirements, financial condition, and other factors considered by the Board. As of March 15, 2023, there were 1,955 holders of record. On February 28, 2022, the Board approved a $5.0 billion share repurchase authorization, replacing the $5.0 billion program approved on February 16, 2021, with no expiration date. During fiscal 2023, the company repurchased and retired 11.8 million shares at a cost of $1.0 billion. In the fourth quarter of fiscal 2023, the company purchased 7,138,475 shares at an average price of $76.91, with $4.125 billion remaining under the program. The company has two reportable segments: Domestic and International. The Domestic segment includes operations in all U.S. states, districts, and territories, as well as Best Buy Health, and brands such as Best Buy, Best Buy Ads, Best Buy Business, CST, Current Health, Geek Squad, Lively, Magnolia, Pacific Kitchen and Home, TechLiquidators, and Yardbird, along with domain names bestbuy.com, currenthealth.com, lively.com, techliquidators.com, and yardbird.com. The International segment includes all operations in Canada under the brands Best Buy, Best Buy Mobile, and Geek Squad, and the domain bestbuy.ca. The company’s fiscal year ends on the Saturday nearest the end of January and includes 52 weeks in fiscal 2023, 2022, and 2021. The business is seasonal, with a large portion of revenue and earnings generated in the fiscal fourth quarter, which includes the majority of the holiday shopping season. Comparable sales is a metric used to evaluate the performance of existing stores, websites, and call centers by measuring net sales changes over a comparable prior period of equivalent length, including revenue from online sales regardless of pickup method, revenue from acquisitions beginning in the first full quarter after the first anniversary, and credit card revenue, gift card breakage, commercial sales, and sales to wholesalers and dealers, while excluding revenue from stores closed more than 14 days, discontinued operations, profit-share revenue from services plans, and foreign currency exchange rate fluctuations (applicable only to the International segment). On November 2, 2021, the company acquired all outstanding shares of Current Health Ltd., and on November 4, 2021, it acquired all outstanding shares of Two Peaks, LLC d/b/a Yardbird Furniture. The results of Current Health and Yardbird are excluded from comparable sales until the first quarter of fiscal 2024. The company believes comparable sales is a meaningful supplemental metric for evaluating revenue performance from existing operations versus new store openings or closures. The method may differ from other retailers. The MD&A includes GAAP financial information and certain non-GAAP financial measures such as constant currency, non-GAAP operating income, non-GAAP effective tax rate, and non-GAAP diluted earnings per share. These non-GAAP measures include adjustments for restructuring charges, goodwill and intangible asset impairments, price-fixing settlements, gains and losses on certain investments, intangible asset amortization, acquisition-related costs, and the tax effect of such items. The company sometimes refers to the impact of foreign currency exchange rate changes or fluctuations, which are differences in exchange rates used to convert International segment results from local currencies to U.S. dollars. “Constant currency” represents results adjusted to exclude foreign currency impacts, calculated as the difference between current and comparable prior period results using current and prior period exchange rates. The company believes disclosing revenue changes in constant currency provides useful supplementary information due to significant currency fluctuations. In fiscal 2023, digital sales comprised 33% of Domestic revenue, up from 19% in fiscal 2020, with sales via phone, chat, and virtual channels remaining significantly higher. Despite this shift, 67% of Domestic revenue was transacted in stores, more than half of identified customers engaged in cross-channel shopping, and over 40% of online sales were picked up in stores. The company plays a key role for vendors as the only national consumer electronics specialty retailer who can showcase new technology and help commercialize it. The company is evolving its omnichannel retail strategy, including its store portfolio, operating model, and digital tools, to provide differentiated customer experiences and enhance omnichannel fulfillment. The company is building customer relationships through membership, including evolving its free My Best Buy program and its paid Best Buy Totaltech membership. In Best Buy Health, the company is nurturing a startup within a large organization, leveraging core assets like Geek Squad to grow the Care at Home space, an emerging part of healthcare. As fiscal 2024 begins, macroeconomic headwinds are expected to result in continued sales pressure due to high inflation and rising interest rates, making near-term impacts difficult to predict. However, the company expects long-term industry growth driven by natural technology upgrade and replacement cycles from the pandemic era, continued vendor innovation, and macro technology trends such as cloud, augmented reality, and expanded broadband access. While product categories have different timing nuances, the company believes they are poised for growth. The company is also expanding into newer categories such as wellness technology, personal electric transportation, outdoor living, and electric car charging. The company remains excited about the industry and its future, noting that there are more technology products than ever in homes, technology is increasingly a necessity, and it believes it is uniquely positioned to serve customers in this innovative space.
